ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-001.prompt: A 78-year-old's forward type is 4+ with anti-A and 0 with anti-B, but reverse typing is 0 with both A1 cells and B cells. What should the MLT do next before assigning an ABO group?

options.a: Issue group A RBCs because the forward type overrides a reverse mismatch
options.b: Report group AB from the reverse and skip further reverse workup
options.c: Resolve the missing reverse antibody before assigning the ABO group
options.d: Switch to group O units and cancel ABO testing on this specimen

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-001.explanation: Forward group A should reverse as 0 with A1 cells and reactive with B cells (anti-B). A missing reverse (both cell lines negative) is a discrepancy, often weakened isoagglutinins in elderly patients. Do not assign ABO or issue type-specific RBCs until the reverse is resolved (history, incubate reverse at room temperature, enhance, check subgroups).

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses forward typing with a finished ABO assignment; a mismatch with reverse is a discrepancy that must be resolved first.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a missing reverse with true group AB; AB reverse is negative with A1 and B cells only when the forward is A and B positive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses discrepancy workup with emergency O-negative release; you still complete ABO testing on a valid specimen.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-002.prompt: A donor types 0 with anti-D at immediate spin but 2+ with anti-D at AHG after 37°C. How should the unit be labeled?

options.a: Rh-positive after weak D testing is complete and reactive
options.b: Rh-negative because the immediate-spin anti-D was nonreactive
options.c: DAT-positive discard; do not label D type on the unit
options.d: Emergency O-negative stock regardless of the donor ABO type

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-002.explanation: Donor weak D (anti-D negative at IS, positive at AHG) is labeled Rh-positive so D-negative recipients are not given D antigen. The recipient rule is different: many facilities treat weak-D patients as Rh-negative for transfusion. Immediate-spin anti-D alone is not the donor labeling endpoint.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses recipient weak-D policy with donor labeling; donors who type weak D must be labeled Rh-positive.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a weak-D AHG reaction with a positive DAT requiring unit discard; weak D is a typing result, not a discard criterion.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses D typing with ABO and emergency inventory; weak D does not convert the unit to O-negative stock.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-003.prompt: A preoperative antibody screen is 2+ with both screening cells at AHG; the autocontrol is negative. What is the next step before selecting RBCs?

options.a: Issue after an immediate-spin crossmatch, skipping identification
options.b: Identify the antibody, then crossmatch antigen-negative units
options.c: Repeat ABO/Rh and issue group-specific uncrossmatched RBCs
options.d: Give washed O-negative RBCs without further antibody workup

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-003.explanation: A positive antibody screen with a negative autocontrol means unexpected alloantibody in the plasma. Identification (panel) comes next so antigen-negative units can be selected and crossmatched. The screen detects antibody; it does not name specificity or prove donor compatibility by itself.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses antibody screen with a finished XM: a positive screen requires identification and AHG-compatible antigen-negative units, not IS-only issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a positive screen with emergency uncrossmatched release; this is a scheduled preoperative workup, not physician-released trauma.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses washing/O-negative RBCs with antibody identification; washing does not remove plasma alloantibody risk in the recipient.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-004.prompt: After 37°C incubation and washing in an antibody screen, why is anti-human globulin added before centrifugation?

options.a: To lyse IgM-coated cells so hemolysis can be graded as the endpoint
options.b: To neutralize complement so clinically insignificant colds disappear
options.c: To enzyme-treat the cells so Duffy antigens are stripped off
options.d: To bridge cell-bound IgG that does not agglutinate in saline

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-004.explanation: Most clinically significant antibodies are IgG. They coat red cells at 37°C but often do not lattice in saline. AHG (anti-IgG ± anti-C3) bridges that bound IgG after washing, producing visible agglutination. Washing first removes unbound globulin that would neutralize AHG (false-negative).

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses AHG agglutination with hemolysis scoring; IgM usually agglutinates at immediate spin without AHG.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses AHG with prewarming or neutralization; AHG detects bound IgG/complement, it does not erase cold antibodies.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses AHG reagent with enzyme treatment (ficin/papain), a different enhancement that can destroy Duffy and MNS antigens.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-005.prompt: A jaundiced term newborn has a 3+ DAT. Mother is group O, D-positive; infant is group A, D-positive. What does the DAT most likely indicate?

options.a: Maternal IgG anti-A coating the infant's red cells (HDFN workup)
options.b: Maternal IgM anti-A that crossed the placenta and coated the infant
options.c: Physiologic jaundice; a positive DAT is expected in every newborn
options.d: Infant anti-B formed in utero coating the infant's own group A cells

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-005.explanation: DAT detects in-vivo coating of red cells. Group O mothers can make IgG anti-A/B that crosses the placenta and coats a group A or B infant (ABO HDFN). Next steps follow SOP (eluate, maternal antibody screen). IgM does not cross the placenta, and physiologic jaundice has a negative DAT.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses IgM with IgG: IgM anti-A does not cross the placenta, so it cannot cause a neonatal DAT.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses physiologic jaundice (immature conjugation, DAT-negative) with immune coating shown by a positive DAT.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses maternal alloantibody with an infant making anti-B; neonates do not coat their own A cells with anti-B.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-006.prompt: A D-negative mother has a negative antibody screen and delivers a D-positive infant. Which RhIG decision is correct?

options.a: Withhold RhIG; delivery itself means she is already immunized to D
options.b: Give RhIG; she is D-negative and not immunized, so anti-D risk remains
options.c: Give RhIG if the infant DAT is already 4+ for anti-D coating
options.d: Give RhIG to the D-positive infant rather than to the D-negative mother

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-006.explanation: RhIG prevents anti-D formation in a D-negative person exposed to D-positive cells. Eligibility: mother is D-negative, not already immunized (no immune anti-D), and the infant (or FMH source) is D-positive. A postpartum dose is still indicated after this delivery; antenatal dosing follows facility protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses exposure with immunization: a negative screen means she has not formed anti-D; RhIG is given to prevent that.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses RhIG eligibility with a positive infant DAT; a 4+ DAT is not required and may reflect ABO HDFN, not anti-D.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses who is at risk: the D-negative mother can form anti-D; the D-positive infant does not receive maternal RhIG.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-007.prompt: Anti-K is identified in a patient. A K-negative donor unit is compatible at immediate spin. What crossmatch is required before issue?

options.a: Immediate-spin crossmatch alone is enough once the unit types K-negative
options.b: Electronic crossmatch may replace serology because K was already named
options.c: AHG (or equivalent) crossmatch of the antigen-negative unit is required
options.d: Skip serologic crossmatch and issue after a visual check of the bag

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-007.explanation: Immediate-spin (or electronic) crossmatch is for patients with a current negative antibody screen and no history of clinically significant antibodies. A positive screen / identified alloantibody requires selection of antigen-negative units plus an AHG crossmatch (or validated equivalent) to detect IgG incompatibility.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses ABO immediate-spin XM with AHG XM; IS does not detect IgG anti-K even if the unit is labeled K-negative.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses electronic crossmatch eligibility: computer XM is not used when unexpected antibodies are present.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses visual inspection with compatibility testing; appearance does not rule out IgG incompatibility.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-008.prompt: A packed RBC unit is found sitting on the bench at 22°C. What storage condition was violated?

options.a: Packed RBCs are stored at 1–6°C, not at room temperature
options.b: Packed RBCs must stay frozen at −18°C until the moment of issue
options.c: Packed RBCs must be agitated continuously, like platelet units
options.d: Packed RBCs may remain at 22°C for 24 hours if the seal is intact

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-008.explanation: Licensed packed RBCs are stored at 1–6°C. Room temperature (20–24°C) is platelet storage, and ≤−18°C is frozen plasma/cryo. Time out of controlled refrigeration is limited by SOP (often a 30-minute / measured-temperature rule); a unit left at 22°C on the bench is not in storage.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses RBC fridge storage with FFP/cryoprecipitate frozen storage at −18°C or colder.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses RBCs with platelets, which need 20–24°C plus continuous agitation.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a brief monitored return-to-stock window with 24 hours at room temperature, which is not RBC storage.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-009.prompt: An apheresis platelet is found in the 1–6°C refrigerator, not on the agitator. Why is that storage incorrect?

options.a: Platelets expire at 30 days when they are kept refrigerated
options.b: Platelets must be frozen at −18°C and thawed like FFP before issue
options.c: Platelets must sit in a 37°C water bath from receipt until issue
options.d: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C with continuous gentle agitation

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-009.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C with continuous agitation for gas exchange and to prevent aggregation, typically up to 5–7 days per product dating. Refrigeration (1–6°C) is for RBCs and thawed plasma, not routine platelet storage; freezing is for FFP/cryo.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses platelet dating (about 5–7 days at room temperature) with 30-day refrigerated storage, which is not used.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses platelets with FFP/cryoprecipitate, which are frozen at −18°C or colder until thawed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses platelet room-temp storage with thawing or warming devices; 37°C water-bath holding is not platelet storage.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-010.prompt: FFP is thawed for a case expected in 90 minutes. How should it be handled compared with packed RBCs?

options.a: Keep FFP frozen in the 1–6°C RBC refrigerator until issue
options.b: Thaw per SOP, then hold thawed plasma at 1–6°C; do not refreeze
options.c: Store thawed FFP at 20–24°C on the platelet agitator until issue
options.d: Refreeze leftover thawed FFP at −18°C to preserve clotting factors

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-010.explanation: FFP is stored frozen at −18°C or colder, then thawed per SOP. After thawing it is kept at 1–6°C (like RBCs) for a limited dating window and is not refrozen. It is not stored in the fridge while still frozen, and it is not a room-temperature agitated product.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses frozen FFP storage (≤−18°C) with RBC refrigerator temperature; FFP is not kept frozen at 1–6°C.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses thawed plasma with platelets (20–24°C with agitation).
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses frozen inventory with thawed plasma: once thawed, FFP is not refrozen for later transfusion.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-011.prompt: At issue, unit number and ABO/Rh match the computer, but the patient's wristband medical record number does not match the request. What should the MLT do?

options.a: Issue the unit if the last name on the wristband is close enough
options.b: Rewrite the unit tag to the wristband number and send the product
options.c: Hold issue until two identifiers match the unit, tag, and request
options.d: Send the unit and let nursing reconcile identifiers on the floor

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-011.explanation: Clerical identification errors cause ABO-incompatible transfusion. Issue requires two independent patient identifiers plus unit number and ABO/Rh matching the tag, request, and records. A wristband/request mismatch is a stop: do not relabel around it or push the check to the bedside after release.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses phonetic name similarity with two-identifier match; name-alone or 'close enough' is not an issue check.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses correcting a discrepancy with forging a match; tags are not rewritten to force the wristband number.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses blood-bank issue with nursing bedside check; both are required, and a known ID mismatch is not released.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-012.prompt: Ten minutes into an RBC transfusion the patient develops fever, back pain, and hemoglobinuria. The unit is stopped. What is the blood bank's first workup step?

options.a: Clerical check, then DAT and visual inspection for hemolysis per SOP
options.b: Restart the same unit slowly after an antipyretic is given on the floor
options.c: Run an antibody panel on plasma from the donor bag as the first test
options.d: Discard the remaining unit in the trash so it cannot be reissued

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-012.explanation: Suspect acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: stop the unit, keep IV access, and notify the blood bank. The initial lab workup is a clerical identification check plus visual inspection for hemolysis and a DAT on a post-transfusion specimen, per SOP. Further tests (repeat ABO/XM, cultures) follow that first pass.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses febrile nonhemolytic reaction treatment with AHTR: fever plus back pain/hemoglobinuria is not 'slow and resume.'
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses first-line clerical/DAT/visual checks with a donor-plasma panel, which is not the opening step.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses stopping the transfusion with destroying evidence; the bag and tubing return to the blood bank for the workup.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-013.prompt: A trauma patient is exsanguinating; type and screen are not finished. Uncrossmatched RBCs are requested now. Correct MLT practice?

options.a: Issue O-negative units with no physician signature because it is trauma
options.b: Issue O-neg or group-specific RBCs as a documented physician release
options.c: Refuse all RBCs until a full AHG crossmatch is completed and signed
options.d: Issue any ABO group from oldest dating without recording the release

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-013.explanation: Emergency uncrossmatched RBCs (O-negative, or group-specific once the ABO is known, per protocol) are a physician-released exception. The MLT issues them with signed documentation, then completes type, screen, and crossmatch on retained segments. It is not unsigned 'trauma privilege' and not a reason to skip records.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses clinical urgency with authorization: the ordering physician still signs for uncrossmatched release.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses routine AHG XM with massive-transfusion exception; delaying all RBCs for AHG can be fatal in exsanguination.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses emergency O-neg/group-specific protocol with issuing unmatched random ABO units without documentation.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-014.prompt: A bleeding patient has fibrinogen 80 mg/dL. The team wants a small-volume product, not several units of plasma. What should the MLT prepare?

options.a: Apheresis platelets, because they are the concentrated fibrinogen product
options.b: Packed RBCs, because residual plasma in the bag replaces fibrinogen
options.c: Whole blood; cryoprecipitate is no longer used for hypofibrinogenemia
options.d: Cryoprecipitate, which packs fibrinogen into a small infusion volume

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-014.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is the concentrated fibrinogen (also factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII, fibronectin) product used when fibrinogen is low and volume overload from FFP is a concern. FFP contains fibrinogen but at plasma concentration, so many units would be needed. Platelets and packed RBCs are not fibrinogen concentrates.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses platelet therapy (count/function) with fibrinogen replacement; platelets are not the fibrinogen concentrate.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses RBC transfusion with coagulation-factor replacement; packed RBCs do not treat a fibrinogen of 80 mg/dL.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses current practice: cryoprecipitate remains the small-volume fibrinogen product versus FFP volume.

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-015.prompt: A panel is 3+ with Jk(a+b−) cells, 1+ with Jk(a+b+) cells, and 0 with Jk(a−) cells at AHG; autocontrol is 0. What is the best interpretation?

options.a: Cold autoantibody; prewarm the panel and ignore the Jk pattern
options.b: Anti-I; expect the strongest reactions with cord red cells
options.c: Anti-Jka showing dosage; crossmatch Jk(a−) antigen-negative units
options.d: Warm autoantibody; all adult cells should be positive, including the auto

ascp-mlt-readiness-check-blood-bank-015.explanation: A negative autocontrol rules out autoantibody. Reactivity only with Jk(a+) cells, stronger with Jk(a+b−) (double-dose) than Jk(a+b+) (single-dose), is anti-Jka with dosage. Select Jk(a−) units and AHG-crossmatch. Cold auto/anti-I would not spare Jk(a−) adult cells this cleanly, and a warm auto would typically react with the autocontrol.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses alloanti-Jka with a cold auto; a negative autocontrol and Jk-specific pattern are not a cold auto to prewarm away.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses Kidd dosage with anti-I, which is usually a cold agglutinin stronger with adult I-positive cells, not a Jk(a) pattern.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses alloantibody with warm auto: warm autos usually have a positive autocontrol, not a clean Jk(a−) negative panel.
